sources.authors: Bachmann HU; Hoffmann A

The patient had been taking 1000 mg/d of carnitine for a period of ten weeks.
after the product was omitted the INR values returned to a stable range (2.4–2.8) for over 4 months.
There is one earlier report of potentiation of acenocoumarol by carnitine in the literature [6], thus confirmed by our observation 10 years later.
The mechanism of interaction is still unknown.

sources.authors: Benvenga S; Ruggeri RM; Russo A; Lapa D; Campenni A; Trimarchi F
quotes: In conclusion, L-carnitine is effective in both reversing and preventing symptoms of hyperthyroidism and has a beneficial effect on bone mineralization.
we assessed whether 2 or 4 g/d oral L-carnitine were able to both reverse and prevent/minimize nine hyperthyroidism- related symptoms
Because hyperthyroidism depletes the body deposits of carnitine and since carnitine has no toxicity, teratogenicity, contraindications and interactions with drugs, carnitine can be of clinical use.

adverse events (12 studies, 1041 participants: RR, 1.14, 95% CI 0.86 to 1.51; I² = 0%; low certainty of evidence)

quotes: The recommended starting dose is 10 to 20 mg/kg dry body weight as a slow 2 to 3 minute bolus injection into the venous return line after each dialysis session.
Initiation of therapy may be prompted by trough (pre-dialysis) plasma levocarnitine concentrations that are below normal (40 to 50 µmol/L).

quotes: Various mild gastrointestinal complaints have been reported during the long-term administration of oral L- or D,L-carnitine; these include transient nausea and vomiting, abdominal cramps, and diarrhea.
Decreasing the dosage often diminishes or eliminates drug-related patient body odor or gastrointestinal symptoms when present.
Tolerance should be monitored very closely during the first week of administration, and after any dosage increases.
Seizures have been reported to occur in patients with or without pre-existing seizure activity receiving either oral or intravenous levocarnitine.
In patients with pre-existing seizure activity, an increase in seizure frequency and/or severity has been reported.
Mild myasthenia has been described only in uremic patients receiving D,L-carnitine.

Reports of INR increase with the use of warfarin have been observed. It is recommended that INR levels be monitored in patients on warfarin therapy after the initiation of treatment with levocarnitine or after dose adjustments.
The safety and efficacy of oral levocarnitine has not been evaluated in patients with renal insufficiency.
may result in accumulation of the potentially toxic metabolites, trimethylamine (TMA) and trimethylamine-N-oxide (TMAO), since these metabolites are normally excreted in the urine.
The recommended oral dosage for adults is 990 mg two or three times a day using the 330 mg tablets, depending on clinical response.
The recommended oral dosage for infants and children is between 50 and 100 mg/kg/day in divided doses, with a maximum of 3 g/day.
There are, however, no adequate and well controlled studies in pregnant women.
this drug should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
Levocarnitine supplementation in nursing mothers has not been specifically studied.
There have been no reports of toxicity from levocarnitine overdosage.
Large doses of levocarnitine may cause diarrhea.
sources.notes: FDA levocarnitine tablet label: GI tolerability, seizures, D,L-myasthenia note, warfarin/INR, renal precaution, pregnancy/nursing, dosing (scopes a, b, c, e)

sources.title: Drug Interactions between levocarnitine and warfarin (Drugs.com)
quotes: Limited data suggest that levocarnitine may potentiate the hypoprothrombinemic effects of warfarin and other coumarin anticoagulants.
There have been isolated case reports of INR increase and/or bleeding in patients treated with warfarin or acenocoumarol following the addition of levocarnitine therapy.
INR levels returned to normal after discontinuation of levocarnitine.
The INR should be checked frequently and anticoagulant dosage adjusted accordingly, particularly following initiation, discontinuation, or change of dosage of levocarnitine.
sources.notes: Professional drug-interaction monograph summarizing the warfarin/coumarin signal (scope c)

sources.title: Comparison of pharmacokinetics of L-carnitine, acetyl-L-carnitine and propionyl-L-carnitine after single oral administration of L-carnitine in healthy volunteers.

L-carnitine has a greater maximum plasma concentration than ALC and PLC.

These findings indicate that short-term oral supplementation of GPLC can enhance peak power production in resistance trained males with significantly less LAC accumulation.

sources.authors: Yahyapoor F; Keshani M; Sedaghat A; Feizi A; Clark CCT; Bagherniya M; Safarian M; Badpeyma M; Norouzy A
quotes: Alanine transaminase (ALT) (0.022), lactate (<0.001), creatinine (Cr) (0.005), and international normalized ratio (INR) (0.049) decreased meaningfully in the intervention vs. control group.
Participants were 54 patients, aged > 18 years, with multiple conditions, randomly assigned to receive 3 g L-carnitine per day or placebo, along with enteral feeding, for 1 week.

sources.authors: Krims-Davis K; Ozola M; Razzivina V; Gukalova B; Konrade I; Dambrova M; Liepinsh E
quotes: Healthy volunteers received either carnitine or an acetylcarnitine supplement (0.5 or 1.5 g).
Acetylcarnitine has significantly lower bioavailability than carnitine.
Approximately 90% of both supplements were metabolized to TMAO, reaching 50 µM in plasma-levels previously found to be associated with adverse health outcomes.
The intake of both supplements resulted in substantial TMAO production, raising potential health concerns.

sources.title: l-Carnitine l-tartrate supplementation favorably affects biochemical markers of recovery from physical exertion in middle-aged men and women.
sources.authors: Ho JY; Kraemer WJ; Volek JS; Fragala MS; Thomas GA; Dunn-Lewis C; Coday M; Häkkinen K; Maresh CM
quotes: the effects of Carnipure tartrate (Lonza, Allendale, NJ) supplementation (total dose of 2 g/d of l-carnitine) on markers of performance and recovery from physical exertion in middle-aged men and women.

Two grams of l-carnitine supplementation had positive effects and significantly (P < or = .05) attenuated biochemical markers of purine metabolism (ie, hypoxanthine, xanthine oxidase), free radical formation (malondialdehyde), muscle tissue disruption (myoglobin, creatine kinase), and muscle soreness after physical exertion.
However, markers of physical performance (ie, strength, power, get up and go) were not affected by supplementation.

sources.title: The effects of L-carnitine L-tartrate supplementation on hormonal responses to resistance exercise and recovery.

it is noteworthy that the extension of treatment seems necessary to prevent symptoms reappearance.

sources.title: Carnitine - Health Professional Fact Sheet
quotes: Healthy children and adults do not need to consume carnitine from food or supplements because the liver and kidneys synthesize sufficient amounts to meet daily needs
Dietary carnitine has a bioavailability of about 63% to 75%
Absorption of supplemental L-carnitine is about 14% to 18%, much less than that of dietary L-carnitine

Carnitine does not have an established tolerable upper intake level. However, doses of approximately 3 g/day of carnitine supplements can cause nausea, vomiting, abdominal cramps, diarrhea, and a fishy body odor
The clinical trials assessed the effectiveness of 1 to 3 g/day acetyl-L-carnitine supplementation or placebo over 12 to 52 weeks in participants with mild to moderate dementia or cognitive decline.
It can also cause muscle weakness in people with uremia and seizures in those with seizure disorders.
Treatment with the anticonvulsants valproic acid, phenobarbital, phenytoin, and carbamazepine reduces blood levels of carnitine
Intravenous L-carnitine administration might help treat valproic acid toxicity in children and adults, although the optimal regimen has not been identified
sources.notes: NIH ODS Health Professional fact sheet: intake, absorption, safety ceiling, interactions (scopes a, b, c, e)

sources.title: Disposition and metabolite kinetics of oral L-carnitine in humans.
sources.authors: Bain MA; Milne RW; Evans AM
quotes: The pharmacokinetics of L-carnitine and its metabolites were investigated in 7 healthy subjects following the oral administration of 0, 0.5, 1, and 2 g 3 times a day for 7 days.

Mean plasma concentrations of L-carnitine across an 8-hour dose interval increased significantly (P < .05) from a baseline of 54.2 +/- 9.3 microM to 80.5 +/- 12.5 microM following the 0.5-g dose; there was no further increase at higher doses.
In conclusion, the pharmacokinetics of oral L-carnitine display nonlinearity above a dose of 0.5 g 3 times a day.
sources.notes: Human dose-escalation PK: nonlinearity above 0.5 g TID; split-dose rationale (scope a)

sources.title: Carnitine and acylcarnitines: pharmacokinetic, pharmacological and clinical aspects.
sources.authors: Reuter SE; Evans AM
quotes: The homeostasis of carnitine is multifaceted with concentrations achieved and maintained by a combination of oral absorption, de novo biosynthesis, carrier-mediated distribution into tissues and extensive, but saturable, renal tubular reabsorption.

sources.title: L-carnitine for valproic acid-induced toxicity.

claims.quote: Severe weakness of lower cranial and girdle muscles has been found in 4 subjects among 20 dialysis patients treated with carnitine in order to correct their high plasma triglyceride level.

claims.claim: The FDA label directs INR monitoring for warfarin patients started on levocarnitine or after dose adjustments, because reports of INR increase with concomitant warfarin use exist.
claims.quote: Reports of INR increase with the use of warfarin have been observed. It is recommended that INR levels be monitored in patients on warfarin therapy after the initiation of treatment with levocarnitine or after dose adjustments.

claims.claim: A published case documents INR destabilization by supplemental carnitine: a 33-year-old on stable acenocoumarol developed an unexpected INR rise to 4.65 after taking 1000 mg/day carnitine for ten weeks, and INR returned to a stable range after the supplement was stopped.
claims.quote: The patient had been taking 1000 mg/d of carnitine for a period of ten weeks.

claims.claim: L-carnitine is a peripheral antagonist of thyroid hormone action: 2 or 4 g/day oral L-carnitine both reversed and prevented hyperthyroid symptoms and benefited bone mineralization in a randomized double-blind trial in TSH-suppressed women.
claims.quote: In conclusion, L-carnitine is effective in both reversing and preventing symptoms of hyperthyroidism and has a beneficial effect on bone mineralization.

claims.claim: Adding combined L-carnitine and selenium to methimazole in Graves' disease reduced required methimazole dosage and hastened TRAb negativity in a randomized trial.
claims.quote: MMI requirements were consistently lower in the Intervention Group, both in average dosage (p = 0.013) and cumulative dose (p = 0.020).

claims.claim: Valproate therapy lowers blood carnitine and raises blood ammonia: meta-analysis shows significantly higher ammonia and significantly lower carnitine levels in VPA-treated versus non-VPA groups.
claims.quote: Compared to that in the non-VPA group, the blood carnitine level in the VPA group was significantly lower.

claims.claim: L-carnitine is commonly recommended in severe valproate poisoning and does not appear harmful, though clear clinical benefit for liver protection or speedier recovery is unproven; prophylactic supplementation is advocated in high-risk pediatric VPA patients.
claims.quote: As it does not appear to be harmful, l-carnitine is commonly recommended in severe VPA poisoning, especially in children, although the clinical benefit in terms of liver protection or hastening of recovery from unconsciousness has not been established clearly.

claims.claim: The FDA label flags renal accumulation: oral levocarnitine safety and efficacy have not been evaluated in renal insufficiency, and chronic high doses in severe renal impairment or ESRD may accumulate the potentially toxic metabolites TMA and TMAO.
claims.quote: The safety and efficacy of oral levocarnitine has not been evaluated in patients with renal insufficiency.

claims.claim: Cochrane (52 RCTs, 3398 dialysis participants) does not support carnitine supplementation for dialysis-related carnitine deficiency, and found it made little or no difference to adverse events.
claims.quote: Although carnitine supplementation may slightly improve anaemia-related markers, carnitine supplementation makes little or no difference to adverse events.

claims.claim: Animal evidence cautions against carnitine in compromised renal function: carnitine-supplemented CKD rats showed worsened disease progression, mineral metabolism biochemistries, and cortical porosity, with no physical-function benefit.
claims.quote: Carnitine supplementation worsened CKD progression, mineral metabolism biochemistries, and cortical porosity and did not have an impact on physical function.

claims.claim: Pregnancy data are inadequate: the FDA label states there are no adequate well-controlled studies in pregnant women and that levocarnitine should be used during pregnancy only if clearly needed.
claims.quote: There are, however, no adequate and well controlled studies in pregnant women.
